ecg-reel-001.question: A 54-year-old man, pre-operative assessment for an inguinal hernia, with no symptoms. What is your interpretation?
options: Sinus bradycardia with first-degree AV block
Sinus rhythm at 64 bpm, normal ECG
Sinus rhythm with left anterior fascicular block
commentaires: A junctional rhythm would not have a positive sinus P wave in lead II preceding each QRS with a normal PR interval.
The rate is above 60 bpm and the PR interval remains below 200 ms.
A P wave that is positive in I–II precedes each narrow QRS, with normal PR, QRS, axis and repolarisation.
The axis remains above −30°: the criteria for left anterior fascicular block (axis ≤ −45°) are not met.
ecg-reel-001.explication: Systematic reading: regular rhythm (RR ≈ 0.93 s, i.e. ≈ 64 bpm), P wave positive in I and II and negative in aVR before each QRS, constant and normal PR interval, narrow QRS complexes. The frontal axis is slightly leftward but remains within normal limits (above −30°): I positive, aVF slightly negative, II positive. No pathological Q waves, normal R-wave progression from V1 to V6, concordant repolarisation. The pitfall is to over-interpret a "slightly left" axis as left anterior fascicular block: this requires an axis between −45° and −90° with a qR pattern in aVL and rS in the inferior leads. PTB-XL tracing annotated "normal ECG" (likelihood 100%).
ecg-reel-001.aRetenir: An axis between −30° and +90° is normal: left anterior fascicular block requires an axis ≤ −45°.

ecg-reel-002.question: A 35-year-old woman with brief palpitations at rest, resolved on arrival. True or false: this tracing shows sinus tachycardia.
commentaires: The rate is about 95 bpm: this is normal sinus rhythm, not tachycardia.
Sinus rhythm at ≈ 95 bpm: the threshold for sinus tachycardia is 100 bpm.
ecg-reel-002.explication: The RR intervals measure about 0.63 s (slightly more than 3 large squares), i.e. ≈ 95 bpm. Each narrow QRS is preceded by a P wave that is positive in I and II: the rhythm is sinus. By convention (AHA/ACC/HRS), sinus tachycardia is defined as a rate above 100 bpm; between 60 and 100 bpm it is normal sinus rhythm. The rest of the tracing is normal (PTB-XL annotation "normal ECG"). A normal ECG between episodes does not rule out a paroxysmal arrhythmia: the diagnosis is made by recording during symptoms (Holter, event monitor).
ecg-reel-002.aRetenir: Sinus tachycardia = sinus rhythm > 100 bpm; a normal ECG between episodes does not exclude a paroxysmal arrhythmia.

ecg-reel-003.question: A 59-year-old man, occupational health check. Estimate the heart rate on this tracing (25 mm/s) and state the method used.
ecg-reel-003.reponseAttendue: About 60 bpm: regular rhythm with an RR interval of about 5 large squares (≈ 0.98 s), so 300/5 ≈ 60 bpm (or 10 QRS complexes in 10 s × 6).
ecg-reel-003.explication: In a regular rhythm, the quickest method is 300 divided by the number of large squares (5 mm = 200 ms) between two QRS complexes: here just under 5 large squares, i.e. ≈ 61 bpm. This can be checked by counting the QRS complexes on the 10-s lead II rhythm strip and multiplying by 6. The rhythm is sinus (positive P wave in lead II before each QRS) and the tracing is annotated normal in PTB-XL. Pitfall: in an irregular rhythm, the "300/number of squares" rule no longer applies and only the 10-s count method is reliable.
ecg-reel-003.aRetenir: Regular rhythm: HR = 300 / number of large squares between two QRS complexes; irregular rhythm: QRS complexes in 10 s × 6.

ecg-reel-004.question: A 78-year-old man being investigated for fatigue, not taking any rate-slowing drugs. What is your interpretation?
options: 2:1 AV block with an atrial rate of 96 bpm
commentaires: Each narrow QRS is preceded by a sinus P wave with a constant PR interval, at ≈ 48 bpm.
No blocked P wave is visible between the QRS complexes, in particular within the T wave.
A junctional escape rhythm would not be preceded by a sinus P wave with a normal PR interval.
2:1 SA block cannot be distinguished from sinus bradycardia on a single tracing: it is unmasked by an abrupt doubling of the rate, which is not seen here.
ecg-reel-004.explication: The rhythm is regular with RR intervals of about 1.25 s (≈ 48 bpm). A P wave that is positive in I, II and aVF precedes each narrow QRS with a constant PR interval: this is sinus bradycardia (< 50 bpm according to the 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS guidelines). The main pitfall with a regular bradycardia is 2:1 AV block: look for a P wave "hidden" in the T wave or in the middle of the RR interval, which is not the case here (smooth T waves, clean isoelectric line). Tracing annotated sinus bradycardia in PTB-XL. Management depends on symptoms and on the search for a cause (drugs, hypothyroidism).
ecg-reel-004.aRetenir: With a regular bradycardia, always look for a blocked P wave hidden in the T wave (2:1 AV block).

ecg-reel-005.question: A 54-year-old man, amateur cyclist, completely asymptomatic, ECG performed for a sports medical certificate. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure, with no treatment or pacing
commentaires: Pacing is not indicated for asymptomatic sinus bradycardia (ESC 2021, class III).
Chronotropic treatment has no justification in the absence of symptoms.
Sinus bradycardia is a common adaptation to endurance training and does not require stopping sport.
Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia, without pauses or conduction disease, requires no treatment.
ecg-reel-005.explication: The tracing shows regular sinus rhythm at about 48 bpm: positive P wave in lead II before each QRS, normal PR interval, narrow QRS complexes, no pauses or block. The axis is borderline left (lead II almost isodiphasic, around −30°), without criteria for left anterior fascicular block (axis ≤ −45°). In an asymptomatic athlete, this is physiological sinus bradycardia (vagal tone). The 2021 ESC and 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS guidelines reserve pacing for symptomatic bradycardia with symptom–rhythm correlation; in asymptomatic patients it is not indicated. Work-up is limited to checking for the absence of exertional symptoms and, if needed, an appropriate chronotropic response on exercise testing.
ecg-reel-005.aRetenir: Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia never justifies cardiac pacing.

ecg-reel-006.question: A 63-year-old man found to have a slow pulse at a pre-anaesthetic consultation. What is the approximate ventricular rate on this tracing (25 mm/s)?
commentaires: 50 bpm would correspond to an RR interval of 6 large squares (1.2 s), shorter than that measured.
The RR intervals measure about 7 large squares (≈ 1.45 s), i.e. ≈ 41 bpm.
60 bpm would correspond to 5 large squares between two QRS complexes.
30 bpm would correspond to an RR interval of 10 large squares (2 s).
ecg-reel-006.explication: The QRS complexes are about 7 large squares apart (≈ 1.45 s): 300/7 ≈ 43, and counting on the long lead II strip gives 7 QRS complexes in 10 s, i.e. ≈ 41 bpm. Each QRS is preceded by a sinus P wave with a constant PR interval: this is marked sinus bradycardia (PTB-XL annotation). At this rate, look for symptoms (presyncope, exertional dyspnoea), an iatrogenic cause (beta-blocker, antiarrhythmic drug) or hypothyroidism, and assess chronotropic incompetence on exercise before any decision.
ecg-reel-006.aRetenir: HR = 300 / number of large squares; sinus bradycardia < 50 bpm calls for a search for symptoms and reversible causes.

ecg-reel-007.question: A 70-year-old man admitted with febrile pneumonia (39 °C). What is your interpretation?
options: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
commentaires: 2:1 flutter would give a rate close to 150 bpm and sawtooth F waves, which are absent here.
Regular rhythm at ≈ 113 bpm, each QRS preceded by a P wave that is positive in lead II and negative in aVR.
In AVNRT, the P wave is hidden in the QRS or retrograde just after it, not a sinus P wave before the QRS.
The RR intervals are perfectly regular and organised P waves are visible.
ecg-reel-007.explication: The rhythm is regular at ≈ 113 bpm. A P wave is seen before each QRS, positive in I, II and aVF and negative in aVR, with a constant PR interval: atrial activation originates from the sinus node. In this febrile setting, sinus tachycardia is a physiological response and is treated by addressing the cause. Pitfalls: do not jump to 2:1 flutter (typical rate ≈ 150 bpm, negative F waves in the inferior leads) or junctional tachycardia (absent or retrograde P wave). PTB-XL tracing annotated sinus tachycardia.
ecg-reel-007.aRetenir: Regular tachycardia with a P wave positive in II/aVF and negative in aVR before each QRS: sinus tachycardia; treat the cause.

ecg-reel-008.question: A 57-year-old woman, routine ECG. True or false: the gradual variation in RR intervals seen on this tracing, with an identical P wave before each QRS, is sinus arrhythmia.
commentaires: The RR intervals vary from ≈ 1.03 to ≈ 1.30 s with P waves of identical morphology and a constant PR interval: sinus arrhythmia.
A cycle length variation of more than 120–160 ms with identical sinus P waves and a fixed PR interval does indeed define sinus arrhythmia.
ecg-reel-008.explication: On the long lead II strip, the RR intervals gradually change from about 1.03 s to 1.30 s, with no premature complexes or abrupt pauses. Each QRS is preceded by a P wave of the same morphology, with a constant PR interval: the pacemaker remains sinus and it is its rate that fluctuates. Respiratory sinus arrhythmia (acceleration on inspiration) is physiological, especially in young people. Differential diagnoses: premature atrial contractions (premature P wave of different morphology) and SA block (pause equal to a multiple of the basic cycle). PTB-XL annotation: sinus arrhythmia, normal ECG.
ecg-reel-008.aRetenir: Sinus arrhythmia = gradual variation in cycle length with identical P waves and a constant PR interval; it is most often physiological.

ecg-reel-009.question: A 61-year-old man with irregular palpitations since the previous day, haemodynamically stable. What is your interpretation?
options: Sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial contractions
Atrial fibrillation with moderate ventricular response
commentaires: There is no reproducible sinus P wave to serve as an underlying rhythm.
No regular sawtooth F waves are visible in II, III, aVF or V1.
This requires at least three distinct P-wave morphologies, which are not present here.
Irregularly irregular RR intervals, no organised P waves, narrow QRS complexes, mean HR ≈ 63 bpm.
ecg-reel-009.explication: The RR intervals vary without any periodicity (from ≈ 0.7 to 1.4 s) and no organised P wave can be identified: this is the ECG definition of atrial fibrillation (ESC 2024), which must be documented on a 12-lead ECG or a tracing of at least 30 s. The QRS complexes are narrow and the mean ventricular response is ≈ 63 bpm. The differential diagnoses of an irregular narrow-QRS rhythm are frequent premature atrial contractions (visible premature P waves), flutter with variable conduction (regular F waves) and multifocal atrial tachycardia (multiple P-wave morphologies). Next steps: assessment of thromboembolic risk (CHA2DS2-VA) and of the rhythm/rate control strategy.
ecg-reel-009.aRetenir: AF = irregularly irregular RR intervals + no organised P waves, to be documented on a 12-lead ECG.

ecg-reel-010.question: A 69-year-old man with an irregular rhythm on auscultation. Which feature of this tracing establishes atrial fibrillation rather than flutter with variable conduction?
options: Chaotic atrial activity, with no regular F waves
The irregularity of the RR intervals
The presence of narrow QRS complexes
A mean ventricular rate below 100 bpm
commentaires: The baseline oscillations vary in amplitude and rate: there is no organised circuit as in flutter.
Flutter with variable conduction also produces irregular RR intervals: this criterion does not distinguish them.
Both AF and flutter are conducted with narrow QRS complexes in the absence of bundle branch block.
The ventricular rate depends on AV nodal conduction, not on the atrial mechanism.
ecg-reel-010.explication: This tracing shows coarse AF: the f waves are clearly visible in II, III and aVF, but their amplitude, morphology and interval change constantly, and the RR intervals are irregularly irregular (≈ 94 bpm on average). In flutter, even with variable conduction, the F waves are regular (≈ 250–350/min), of constant morphology, and the RR intervals are often multiples of the same cycle. The pitfall is to call every coarse AF "flutter": what matters is the regularity of atrial activity, not its amplitude. PTB-XL annotation: atrial fibrillation.
ecg-reel-010.aRetenir: AF or flutter: the regularity of atrial activity (identical, regular F waves) settles it, not the irregularity of the RR intervals.

ecg-reel-011.question: An 81-year-old man with no significant history and palpitations for a few days. After interpreting this tracing, what is the management for thromboembolic prevention?
options: No treatment, as the score is zero
Oral anticoagulation, preferably with a DOAC
Anticoagulation only if AF becomes permanent
commentaires: Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF.
Age ≥ 75 years scores 2 points on CHA2DS2-VA: the score is not zero.
AF with a CHA2DS2-VA score of 2 (age ≥ 75 years): anticoagulation is recommended, with a DOAC as first-line therapy.
The indication depends on thromboembolic risk, not on whether AF is paroxysmal or permanent.
ecg-reel-011.explication: The tracing shows atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular RR intervals (≈ 90 bpm), no P waves, fine baseline oscillations, narrow QRS complexes. According to the 2024 ESC guidelines, thromboembolic risk is assessed with the CHA2DS2-VA score (sex is no longer counted): age ≥ 75 years alone scores 2 points, which mandates oral anticoagulation (class I), with DOACs preferred over VKAs except in patients with a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis. The type of AF (paroxysmal, persistent, permanent) does not change the indication. Aspirin has no role in this indication.
ecg-reel-011.aRetenir: AF and age ≥ 75 years: CHA2DS2-VA ≥ 2, oral anticoagulation (preferably a DOAC), whatever the type of AF.

ecg-reel-012.question: An 83-year-old man with recent exertional dyspnoea. Which statements correctly describe this tracing?
options: The RR intervals are irregularly irregular
Sawtooth F waves are visible in lead II
No organised P wave can be identified
There is a pause of more than 3 seconds
commentaires: The RR intervals vary from ≈ 0.6 to 1.2 s without any periodicity.
There is no regular sawtooth atrial activity: this is not flutter.
The baseline shows fine irregular undulations, with no reproducible P wave.
The longest RR interval measures about 1.2 s.
The QRS duration is under 120 ms: no associated bundle branch block.
ecg-reel-012.explication: This is atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular response (≈ 73 bpm on average): irregularly irregular RR intervals, no P waves, fine baseline oscillations ("fine" AF), narrow QRS complexes. No significant pause is recorded during these 10 seconds. The absence of regular F waves rules out flutter. In this elderly, breathless patient, ventricular function (echocardiography), rate control on exertion and anticoagulation (age ≥ 75 years) should be assessed. PTB-XL annotation: atrial fibrillation.
ecg-reel-012.aRetenir: Fine AF: the baseline may look almost flat; it is the total irregularity of the RR intervals that points to the diagnosis.

ecg-reel-013.question: A 23-year-old woman with rapid palpitations for 2 hours, normal blood pressure. What is your interpretation?
commentaires: Sinus tachycardia is regular, with a P wave visible before each QRS.
AVNRT is a strictly regular tachycardia.
2:1 flutter is regular, typically at around 150 bpm.
Narrow-QRS tachycardia, irregularly irregular (RR 0.38 to 0.60 s), with no organised P waves.
ecg-reel-013.explication: The mean rate is ≈ 114 bpm with completely irregular RR intervals (0.38 to 0.60 s) and no organised P waves: this is atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response and narrow QRS complexes. The first question with a narrow-QRS tachycardia is "regular or irregular?": regular tachycardias (sinus, AVNRT or AVRT, 2:1 flutter) are distinguished from AF. In a 23-year-old patient, AF should prompt a search for a cause (hyperthyroidism, alcohol, structural heart disease, pre-excitation — here narrow QRS without a delta wave). PTB-XL annotation: atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response.
ecg-reel-013.aRetenir: Narrow-QRS tachycardia: first ask "regular or irregular?"; irregular = AF until proven otherwise.

ecg-reel-014.question: A 64-year-old man with an irregular rhythm. Estimate the mean ventricular rate on this tracing and justify your method.
ecg-reel-014.reponseAttendue: About 90 bpm: 15 QRS complexes on the 10-s long lead II strip × 6. In an irregular rhythm (here atrial fibrillation), the "300/number of squares" rule cannot be used.
ecg-reel-014.explication: The rhythm is atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular RR intervals from 0.49 to 1.0 s, no organised P waves). In this case, measuring a single RR interval would give a misleading rate (from 60 to 120 bpm depending on the cycle chosen). The recommended method is to count the QRS complexes over a known duration: 15 QRS complexes on the 10-s long lead II strip, i.e. ≈ 90 bpm. In AF, the initial rate control target is a resting HR < 110 bpm (lenient control), tightened if symptoms persist (ESC 2024). The PTB-XL report also mentions incomplete right bundle branch block.
ecg-reel-014.aRetenir: In an irregular rhythm, measure the rate by counting QRS complexes over 10 s (× 6), never from a single RR interval.

ecg-reel-015.question: A 75-year-old woman with palpitations and dyspnoea for 24 hours. What is your interpretation?
commentaires: No discrete sinus P wave precedes the QRS complexes; atrial activity is continuous in the inferior leads.
AVNRT does not explain the undulating atrial activity visible between the QRS complexes.
Regular tachycardia at ≈ 141 bpm with sawtooth atrial activity at ≈ 280/min in the inferior leads.
The QRS complexes are narrow and identical to the usual QRS: this is not VT.
ecg-reel-015.explication: The tachycardia is strictly regular at ≈ 141 bpm (RR 0.42 s) with narrow QRS complexes. In II, III and aVF, the baseline is never isoelectric: one F wave can be made out between two QRS complexes and another hidden in the QRS or T wave, i.e. atrial activity at ≈ 280/min conducted 2:1. Any regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at around 140–150 bpm should raise suspicion of 2:1 flutter; vagal manoeuvres or adenosine, by transiently slowing conduction, unmask the F waves. Flutter requires the same thromboembolic risk assessment as AF. PTB-XL annotation: atrial flutter with 2:1 block.
ecg-reel-015.aRetenir: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at around 140–150 bpm: think of 2:1 flutter and look for F waves in II, III, aVF and V1.

ecg-reel-016.question: A 60-year-old man with palpitations for 3 days. What is the most likely mechanism of this arrhythmia?
options: AV nodal re-entry using the slow and fast pathways
Right atrial macro-re-entry dependent on the cavotricuspid isthmus
A rapidly firing automatic focus in the left atrium
AV re-entry via an accessory pathway
commentaires: AVNRT does not produce continuous sawtooth atrial activity at 300/min.
Negative sawtooth F waves in the inferior leads and positive F waves in V1: typical counterclockwise flutter, circulating around the tricuspid annulus.
A focal tachycardia produces P waves separated by an isoelectric line, not a sawtooth pattern.
Orthodromic re-entry produces a retrograde P wave after each QRS, without 2:1 atrial activity.
ecg-reel-016.explication: The tracing shows a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at 150 bpm, with negative sawtooth F waves in II, III and aVF without return to the isoelectric line, and positive F waves in V1: this is the pattern of typical "counterclockwise" flutter conducted 2:1 (atrial rate ≈ 300/min). The circuit is a right atrial macro-re-entry around the tricuspid annulus, passing through the cavotricuspid isthmus. CTI ablation is highly effective (> 90%) and recommended for recurrent or symptomatic typical flutter (ESC 2019). Thromboembolic prevention follows the same rules as for AF. PTB-XL annotation: atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction.
ecg-reel-016.aRetenir: Typical counterclockwise flutter: negative sawtooth F waves in the inferior leads, positive in V1; curative treatment = cavotricuspid isthmus ablation.

ecg-reel-017.question: A 65-year-old man being investigated for a slow, irregular pulse. What is your interpretation?
options: Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
Sinus rhythm with Mobitz I second-degree AV block
commentaires: Regular, identical F waves (≈ 300/min) in the inferior leads, with conduction ratios that change from one cycle to the next.
Atrial activity is organised and regular, which excludes AF.
There is no sinus P wave separated by an isoelectric line, but a continuous undulation.
This involves P waves of different morphologies separated by an isoelectric line.
ecg-reel-017.explication: The RR intervals are irregular (0.82 to 1.6 s, ≈ 54 bpm) but atrial activity is perfectly regular: in II, III and aVF, identical F waves about 200 ms apart (≈ 300/min) are seen between the QRS complexes, with no isoelectric line. The QRS complexes occur after 4 to 8 F waves depending on the cycle: this is flutter with variable conduction. The pitfall is to diagnose AF because the RR intervals are irregular: always look at the atrial activity. Slow, variable conduction without rate-slowing drugs may indicate AV nodal disease. PTB-XL annotation: atrial flutter with variable conduction.
ecg-reel-017.aRetenir: Irregular RR intervals do not mean AF: regular, identical F waves indicate flutter with variable conduction.

ecg-reel-018.question: A 70-year-old man with ill-defined palpitations. What is the predominant atrioventricular conduction ratio on this tracing?
commentaires: Four F waves (≈ 270/min) per QRS on most cycles (RR ≈ 0.9 s).
With 2:1 conduction, the ventricular rate would be about 135 bpm, not 68 bpm.
Only the last, shorter cycle (≈ 0.65 s) corresponds to 3:1 conduction.
1:1 conduction of flutter would give a ventricular rate of about 270 bpm.
ecg-reel-018.explication: In II, III and aVF, regular sawtooth F waves are seen about 220–225 ms apart (≈ 270/min). Between two QRS complexes (RR ≈ 0.9 s, HR ≈ 68 bpm), there are four F waves: conduction is 4:1, with a shorter last cycle at 3:1. Spontaneous 4:1 conduction reflects AV nodal slowing, either physiological or drug-induced. Method: divide the atrial rate by the ventricular rate, or count the F waves between two QRS complexes, not forgetting the one hidden in the QRS or T wave. PTB-XL annotation: atrial flutter with 4:1 block.
ecg-reel-018.aRetenir: Flutter conduction ratio = atrial rate / ventricular rate; remember the F wave hidden in the QRS or T wave.

ecg-reel-019.question: A 77-year-old man with bradycardia found at a clinic visit, with few symptoms. What is your interpretation?
options: Slow atrial flutter with variable conduction
commentaires: Atrial activity is continuous and regular, with no sinus P wave followed by a premature P wave.
Regular, identical atrial waves at ≈ 215/min in III and aVF, with variable conduction (≈ 47 bpm).
With 2:1 block, there would be exactly two P waves per QRS with regular RR intervals, which is not the case.
The atrial oscillations are regular and of constant morphology.
ecg-reel-019.explication: The RR intervals alternate between ≈ 1.1 and 1.5 s (≈ 47 bpm). In III and aVF, there is regular atrial activity of constant morphology, about 280 ms apart (≈ 215/min), slower than in untreated typical flutter (250–350/min). The QRS complexes occur after 4 to 6 F waves: variable conduction. "Slow" flutter is seen with antiarrhythmic drugs (class IC or amiodarone) or with atrial cardiomyopathy; it carries a risk of 1:1 conduction if the atrial cycle length increases further. The pitfall is to mistake these waves for sinus P waves. PTB-XL annotation: slow atrial flutter.
ecg-reel-019.aRetenir: Flutter can be slow (< 250/min) on antiarrhythmic drugs: the regular, repetitive pattern of atrial activity remains the key.

ecg-reel-020.question: An 80-year-old man reporting "skipped beats". What is your interpretation?
commentaires: An aberrant PAC would be preceded by a premature P wave, which is absent here.
There is no blocked P wave: the extra complexes are premature wide QRS complexes.
Each sinus QRS is followed by a premature wide complex, not preceded by a P wave, and then a compensatory pause.
The wide complexes are isolated and premature, not a run of ventricular beats.
ecg-reel-020.explication: The rhythm alternates regularly between a narrow sinus QRS (preceded by a P wave) and a premature wide QRS (coupling interval ≈ 0.48 s), not preceded by a P wave, with discordant repolarisation, followed by a long pause of ≈ 1.4 s: this is ventricular bigeminy. This pause corresponds to the usual compensatory pause of PVCs: the PVC does not reset the sinus node, whose next P wave falls in the ventricular refractory period. Management depends on the PVC burden on Holter monitoring, symptoms and the search for underlying structural heart disease (ESC 2022). PTB-XL annotation: premature ventricular contractions, bigeminy.
ecg-reel-020.aRetenir: PVC: premature wide QRS, not preceded by a P wave, followed by a compensatory pause.

ecg-reel-021.question: A 69-year-old man; the nurse counts a radial pulse of 36 bpm while the monitor displays 72 bpm. What explanation does this tracing provide?
options: The monitor is double-counting tall T waves
This is 2:1 AV block with P waves counted as QRS
The true rate is 36 bpm; the monitor is wrong
The early PVCs of bigeminy eject little blood
commentaires: The tracing shows genuine premature wide QRS complexes, not a T wave counted in error.
The extra complexes are wide QRS complexes, not blocked P waves.
The ECG does show 72 QRS complexes per minute, half of which are PVCs.
Every other beat is an early PVC, occurring before adequate filling: the pulse wave is absent or very weak.
ecg-reel-021.explication: The tracing shows ventricular bigeminy: each narrow sinus QRS is followed by a wide PVC (positive in the inferior leads), then a pause. The electrical rate is 72 bpm, but the early PVCs (coupling interval ≈ 0.63 s) occur before adequate ventricular filling and generate little or no pulse wave: this is the "pulse deficit". The palpated pulse (36 bpm) may wrongly suggest severe bradycardia. Conversely, a monitor may overcount tall T waves; hence the importance of looking at the tracing. PTB-XL annotation: PVCs in bigeminy.
ecg-reel-021.aRetenir: Ventricular bigeminy: the palpated pulse is often half the electrical rate (PVCs eject little blood).

ecg-reel-022.question: A 53-year-old man with isolated palpitations at rest. Which feature of this tracing supports a ventricular origin of the premature complexes?
options: QRS identical to the sinus QRS, preceded by a P wave
Non-compensatory pause with sinus node reset
Wide QRS, no premature P wave, compensatory pause
Occurrence after a P wave with a prolonged PR
commentaires: This would describe a normally conducted premature atrial contraction.
A non-compensatory pause is the classic argument for a PAC, not a PVC.
Both premature complexes are wide, not preceded by a P wave, and bracketed by an interval close to two basic cycles.
A QRS conducted after a P wave with a prolonged PR interval suggests AV conduction, not a PVC.
ecg-reel-022.explication: Two premature complexes are visible (at about 7 and 9 s). They are wide, of different morphology from the sinus QRS complexes, not preceded by a premature P wave, with a discordant T wave. Around the first one, coupling interval (≈ 0.49 s) + pause (≈ 0.94 s) ≈ 1.42 s, close to two basic cycles (≈ 2 × 0.74 s): (near-)compensatory pause. These three features point to PVCs. Conversely, a PAC is preceded by a premature P wave, usually has a narrow QRS identical to the baseline QRS, and is followed by a non-compensatory pause. PTB-XL annotation: premature ventricular contractions.
ecg-reel-022.aRetenir: PVC: wide QRS, no premature P wave, compensatory pause; PAC: premature P wave, narrow QRS, non-compensatory pause.

ecg-reel-023.question: A 73-year-old man, routine ECG. True or false: the premature wide complex recorded on this tracing is followed by a compensatory pause.
commentaires: Coupling interval (≈ 0.50 s) + pause (≈ 1.20 s) ≈ 1.70 s, i.e. about two sinus cycles (≈ 2 × 0.86 s).
The sum of the coupling interval and the pause is indeed about two basic RR intervals: the pause is compensatory.
ecg-reel-023.explication: The premature complex occurs at about 3 s: it is wide, not preceded by a P wave, with discordant repolarisation (PVC). To assess the pause, measure the interval between the QRS preceding and the QRS following the PVC: ≈ 0.50 + 1.20 = 1.70 s, for a basic sinus cycle of ≈ 0.86 s (2 cycles = 1.72 s). The pause is therefore compensatory: the PVC has not penetrated the sinus node, whose rhythm continues; the next sinus P wave falls in the ventricular refractory period. PTB-XL annotation: premature ventricular contraction.
ecg-reel-023.aRetenir: Compensatory pause: the interval bracketing the premature beat equals two basic cycles.

ecg-reel-024.question: A 65-year-old woman with a sensation of "thumps" in the chest. What is the most likely nature of the premature beats?
commentaires: Narrow QRS complexes identical to the sinus QRS, with a non-compensatory pause.
PVCs would have wide QRS complexes of different morphology.
An escape beat is late (after a pause), never premature.
There is no ventricular tachycardia on this tracing.
ecg-reel-024.explication: The underlying rhythm is sinus (≈ 68 bpm, RR ≈ 0.88 s). Two beats occur prematurely (coupling interval ≈ 0.56–0.57 s) with a narrow QRS of the same morphology as the sinus QRS complexes. The bracketing interval (≈ 0.56 + 1.04 = 1.60 s) is shorter than two basic cycles (1.76 s): the pause is non-compensatory, because the PAC has "reset" the sinus node. The premature P wave may be distorted or hidden in the preceding T wave, hence the value of comparing T waves. Isolated PACs are usually benign, but a high burden is associated with a subsequent risk of AF. PTB-XL annotation: premature atrial contractions.
ecg-reel-024.aRetenir: PAC: premature narrow QRS, premature P wave often hidden in the T wave, non-compensatory pause.

ecg-reel-025.question: A 71-year-old man with palpitations. True or false: the pauses following the premature narrow complexes on this tracing are non-compensatory, which points to premature atrial contractions.
commentaires: Coupling interval (≈ 0.56 s) + pause (≈ 1.04 s) ≈ 1.60 s, shorter than two basic cycles (≈ 1.76 s): non-compensatory pause.
The sum of coupling interval and pause is indeed shorter than two basic RR intervals, which is typical of a PAC.
ecg-reel-025.explication: Three premature complexes with narrow QRS, of the same morphology as the sinus QRS complexes, occur with a coupling interval of ≈ 0.56 s. The bracketing interval (≈ 1.60 s) is shorter than two sinus cycles (≈ 1.76 s): the pause is non-compensatory. The PAC depolarises the sinus node, which starts a new cycle; hence this shortening. A PVC, which usually does not penetrate the sinus node, leaves a compensatory pause. This criterion is useful but not absolute: a PVC may be interpolated, and a PAC may fail to reset the sinus node. PTB-XL annotation: premature atrial contractions.
ecg-reel-025.aRetenir: Non-compensatory pause (< 2 cycles): an argument in favour of a premature atrial contraction.

ecg-reel-026.question: A 65-year-old man with palpitations of abrupt onset 30 minutes ago, BP 125/80 mmHg, no adverse features. What is the recommended first therapeutic step?
options: Vagal manoeuvres, then IV adenosine if they fail
commentaires: Electrical cardioversion is reserved for unstable patients or failure of pharmacological measures.
Amiodarone is not the first-line treatment for a stable regular narrow-QRS tachycardia.
Digoxin has no role in the acute termination of a junctional tachycardia.
Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia in a stable patient: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine (ESC 2019, class I).
ecg-reel-026.explication: The tracing shows a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at ≈ 172 bpm (RR 0.35 s), with no visible P wave before the QRS complexes and no sawtooth atrial activity: the appearance of a re-entrant junctional tachycardia (AVNRT or AVRT). In a stable patient, the 2019 ESC guidelines recommend vagal manoeuvres first (ideally the modified Valsalva manoeuvre, with leg elevation), then IV adenosine (class I); if these fail, IV verapamil/diltiazem or a beta-blocker (class IIa), and cardioversion if the patient becomes unstable. Recording an ECG during adenosine administration aids diagnosis (unmasking flutter or atrial tachycardia). PTB-XL annotation: paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.
ecg-reel-026.aRetenir: Stable regular narrow-QRS tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres, then IV adenosine, with continuous ECG recording.

ecg-reel-027.question: A 29-year-old woman with palpitations of abrupt onset and offset since adolescence, currently in an episode. What is the most likely mechanism of this tachycardia?
commentaires: 2:1 flutter typically gives a ventricular rate close to 150 bpm and visible F waves.
Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at 200 bpm with no visible P wave (retrograde P wave hidden in the QRS) in a young woman: AVNRT is the most likely.
Sinus tachycardia at 200 bpm at rest is excluded and would be accompanied by a visible sinus P wave.
Fascicular VT produces relatively wide QRS complexes with an RBBB pattern and left axis deviation, not normal narrow QRS complexes.
ecg-reel-027.explication: Strictly regular tachycardia at ≈ 200 bpm (RR ≈ 0.29–0.30 s), narrow QRS complexes identical to a normal QRS, with no P wave visible before the QRS: retrograde atrial activation is simultaneous with the QRS, which is typical of common (slow–fast) AVNRT, the most frequent junctional tachycardia, with a female predominance. Orthodromic AVRT would more likely show a retrograde P wave in the ST segment (RP > 70 ms). Curative treatment is slow pathway ablation (success rate > 95%, risk of AV block < 1%). PTB-XL annotation: paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.
ecg-reel-027.aRetenir: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia with no visible P wave in a young woman: AVNRT until proven otherwise.

ecg-reel-028.question: A 78-year-old woman with rapid palpitations for 1 hour, haemodynamically stable. Which statements about this tracing are correct?
options: The QRS appearance means it must be treated as VT
It is a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia
The irregularity of the RR intervals suggests AF
The ventricular rate is about 160 bpm
Delta waves are visible on the QRS complexes
commentaires: The QRS complexes are narrow: this is not a wide-QRS tachycardia.
The RR intervals are constant (≈ 0.375 s) and the QRS duration is under 120 ms.
The RR intervals are perfectly regular.
An RR interval of ≈ 0.375 s corresponds to 60/0.375 ≈ 160 bpm.
The QRS complexes show no initial slurring: no visible pre-excitation.
ecg-reel-028.explication: Strictly regular tachycardia at ≈ 160 bpm (RR ≈ 0.375 s) with narrow QRS complexes and no clearly identifiable P wave before the QRS. Possible diagnoses are AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT, atrial tachycardia and 2:1 flutter (compatible rate): an ECG recorded during a vagal manoeuvre or adenosine will settle the question (abrupt termination = re-entry involving the AV node; unmasking of F or P waves = atrial arrhythmia). There is no irregularity (AF), no wide QRS (VT, aberrancy) and no delta wave. PTB-XL annotation: paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.
ecg-reel-028.aRetenir: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia: adenosine with ECG recording is both a treatment and a diagnostic test.

ecg-reel-029.question: An 81-year-old woman being investigated for falls. Which atrioventricular conduction abnormality does this tracing show?
commentaires: There is neither progressive PR prolongation nor a blocked P wave.
Each P wave is conducted with a constant PR interval of about 260 ms (> 200 ms).
Each P wave is followed by a QRS.
Pre-excitation shortens the PR interval (< 120 ms): here it is prolonged.
ecg-reel-029.explication: Regular sinus rhythm at ≈ 63 bpm. The low-amplitude P wave is seen in II and V1 well before the QRS, separate from the end of the T wave; the PR interval measures about 6.5 small squares, i.e. ≈ 260 ms, constant from cycle to cycle, and every P wave is conducted. This is first-degree AV block (PR > 200 ms). Precordial voltages are also high (tall R waves in V5–V6), as noted in PTB-XL. Isolated and asymptomatic first-degree AV block does not justify pacing; in a patient with falls, however, a more severe paroxysmal conduction disorder should be sought (Holter, repeat ECGs). PTB-XL annotation: first-degree AV block.
ecg-reel-029.aRetenir: First-degree AV block = constant PR > 200 ms with all P waves conducted; in isolation, it does not justify pacing.

ecg-reel-030.question: A 67-year-old man, ECG before starting a beta-blocker. Measure the PR interval and draw your conclusion.
ecg-reel-030.reponseAttendue: PR ≈ 270–280 ms (≈ 7 small squares), constant, all P waves conducted: first-degree AV block; caution with AV nodal blocking drugs (monitor the PR interval).
ecg-reel-030.explication: In lead II, the P wave is clearly distinct after the T wave; from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS, there are about 7 small squares, i.e. ≈ 270–280 ms, identical on all cycles, with sinus rhythm at ≈ 73 bpm and narrow QRS complexes. This is first-degree AV block (PR > 200 ms), described as "marked" in the PTB-XL report. Drugs that slow AV nodal conduction (beta-blockers, rate-limiting calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone) may worsen it: a repeat ECG after starting treatment is prudent. A very long PR interval (> 300 ms) can by itself cause symptoms through loss of AV synchrony ("pseudo-pacemaker syndrome").
ecg-reel-030.aRetenir: The PR interval is measured from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS; > 200 ms = first-degree AV block, to be monitored on AV nodal blocking drugs.

ecg-reel-031.question: A 58-year-old man with recurrent presyncope for a week. What is the conduction disorder?
options: Complete AV block with ventricular escape
commentaires: The PR interval of the conducted P waves is fixed: there is no atrioventricular dissociation.
There is no progressive PR prolongation before the blocked P wave.
The P waves are at ≈ 110/min: it is AV conduction that is failing, not the sinus node.
One P wave in three is conducted with a constant PR interval; the other P waves are blocked.
ecg-reel-031.explication: The P waves, clearly visible in II, III and aVF, are regular at ≈ 110/min. The QRS complexes are regular at ≈ 37 bpm (RR 1.6 s): of every three P waves, only one is conducted, always with the same PR interval (≈ 200 ms), one of the blocked P waves being partly hidden in the T wave. The constant PR interval of the conducted beats distinguishes this high-grade second-degree AV block (3:1) from complete AV block (variable PR, dissociation). The QRS complexes also show an intraventricular conduction delay with right axis deviation (PTB-XL annotation). Symptomatic high-grade second-degree AV block without a reversible cause is an indication for permanent pacing (ESC 2021, class I).
ecg-reel-031.aRetenir: Fixed PR interval of conducted beats = second-degree AV block (here 3:1); variable PR with dissociation = third-degree AV block.

ecg-reel-032.question: An 88-year-old woman with a collapse and fall. What is your interpretation?
options: Complete AV block with an escape rhythm at 40 bpm
commentaires: The P waves (≈ 98/min) and QRS complexes (≈ 40 bpm) each beat at their own rate with a variable PR interval: complete AV dissociation.
In 2:1 AV block, the conducted P waves would have a constant PR interval, which is not the case.
The P waves are much faster than the QRS complexes: the sinus rate is not slow.
The P waves are positive in lead II, regular and independent of the QRS complexes, not retrograde.
ecg-reel-032.explication: The P waves are regular at ≈ 98/min (clearly visible in II and V1); the QRS complexes are regular at ≈ 40 bpm (RR ≈ 1.5 s). The position of the P wave relative to the QRS changes with each cycle (P just before, within or after the QRS): there is no fixed relationship; this is complete atrioventricular dissociation due to third-degree AV block. The escape rhythm has a right-sided delay pattern in V1 (PTB-XL annotation: incomplete RBBB). In a symptomatic patient, permanent pacing is clearly indicated once a reversible cause has been excluded (ESC 2021, class I); in the meantime, continuous monitoring and temporary pacing if needed.
ecg-reel-032.aRetenir: Third-degree AV block: P waves faster than the QRS complexes, with no fixed relationship between them (variable PR), regular escape rhythm.

ecg-reel-033.question: A 68-year-old man with dyspnoea and fatigue for 2 weeks. Which statements are correct?
options: The P waves are dissociated from the QRS complexes
The underlying rhythm is slow atrial fibrillation
The narrow-QRS escape rhythm suggests a proximal level of block
Atropine is the definitive treatment for this disorder
Permanent pacing is indicated in the absence of a reversible cause
commentaires: The P waves (≈ 82/min) and QRS complexes (≈ 38 bpm) have no fixed relationship.
Regular P waves are visible: the atrial rhythm is sinus.
A narrow-QRS escape rhythm most often arises from the junction (AV node–His bundle).
Atropine is only a temporary measure and is often ineffective in infranodal block.
Acquired complete AV block, whether symptomatic or not, is an indication for pacing (ESC 2021, class I).
ecg-reel-033.explication: The P waves, of low amplitude but regular (≈ 82/min), are visible in II and V1; the narrow QRS complexes are regular at ≈ 38 bpm (RR ≈ 1.57 s) and the PR interval changes with each cycle: complete AV block with a narrow-QRS escape rhythm. A narrow, relatively fast escape rhythm suggests nodal or proximal His block; a wide, slow escape rhythm (< 40 bpm) suggests infra-Hisian block, which is less stable. The axis is deviated to the right (PTB-XL annotation). Non-reversible acquired complete AV block is an indication for permanent pacing (ESC 2021). Atropine and isoprenaline are only bridging measures.
ecg-reel-033.aRetenir: Third-degree AV block: narrow escape = rather proximal block; wide, slow escape = distal block, more dangerous; in both cases, permanent pacing.

ecg-reel-034.question: A 73-year-old man, pre-operative ECG. Which intraventricular conduction disorder is present?
commentaires: LBBB would give a QS or rS pattern in V1 and a broad notched R wave in V6.
The axis is normal and the QRS is widened with a right-sided delay pattern.
QRS ≥ 120 ms with an rsR' pattern in V1 and a broad, slurred S wave in V6.
The QRS duration is 120 ms or more: the block is complete.
ecg-reel-034.explication: In V1, the QRS has an rsR' pattern with a broad, tall R' wave, followed by a negative T wave (expected secondary change); in V6 and I, the terminal S wave is broad and slurred. The QRS duration is about 130–140 ms. These are the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS criteria for complete right bundle branch block: QRS ≥ 120 ms, rsR' in V1–V2 with R' wider than R, and a widened terminal S wave (> 40 ms or wider than R) in I and V6. The frontal axis is normal: no associated fascicular block. In isolation, RBBB is common and often of no consequence, but depending on the context should prompt a search for right heart disease. PTB-XL annotation: complete RBBB.
ecg-reel-034.aRetenir: Complete RBBB: QRS ≥ 120 ms, rsR' in V1, broad S wave in I and V6.

ecg-reel-035.question: An 86-year-old man being investigated for dyspnoea. In which lead is the characteristic pattern of the conduction disorder on this tracing best seen?
commentaires: V6 shows the broad S wave, an associated but less specific criterion.
aVL is not a key lead for recognising right bundle branch block.
Lead III gives information on the axis but not on the type of bundle branch block.
V1 shows the rsR' ("M-shaped") pattern typical of right bundle branch block.
ecg-reel-035.explication: This tracing shows complete right bundle branch block: in V1, an rsR' pattern with a dominant, widened R' wave; in I and V6, a broad terminal S wave. Lead V1, facing the right ventricle, records the late, slow activation of this ventricle as a positive terminal R' wave. Reading reflex: with a QRS ≥ 120 ms, look at V1 (terminal R' = right-sided delay; QS/rS = left-sided delay), then at I and V6 to confirm. The axis here is slightly leftward, without reaching −45°. PTB-XL annotation: complete RBBB.
ecg-reel-035.aRetenir: Wide QRS: look at V1 first — terminal R' = right bundle branch block, QS or deep rS = left bundle branch block.

ecg-reel-036.question: A 65-year-old man being investigated for a single syncopal episode. What is the most accurate description of the conduction disorders on this tracing?
options: Complete RBBB with left anterior fascicular block
Complete RBBB with left posterior fascicular block
Isolated complete RBBB, normal frontal axis
Left bundle branch block with a normal axis
commentaires: This would require an axis ≤ −45° with rS in II, III and aVF: here the axis is normal.
This would require an axis ≥ +90° with rS in I: here lead I is positive.
rsR' in V1 and broad S wave in V6, with a normal frontal axis (≈ +60°): no associated fascicular block.
The V1 pattern (terminal R') is that of right-sided, not left-sided, delay.
ecg-reel-036.explication: In V1, an rsR' pattern with a dominant R'; in I and V6, a widened terminal S wave: complete right bundle branch block (QRS ≈ 120 ms). In the frontal plane, I and aVF are positive and II has the largest amplitude: axis ≈ +60°, i.e. normal. There is neither left anterior fascicular block (axis ≤ −45°) nor left posterior fascicular block (axis ≥ +90° after other causes have been excluded): this is not bifascicular block. In a patient who has had syncope, bifascicular block would point towards an EP study; isolated RBBB does not carry the same significance. PTB-XL annotation: complete RBBB.
ecg-reel-036.aRetenir: With RBBB, always determine the axis: RBBB + axis ≤ −45° (LAFB) or ≥ +90° (LPFB) = bifascicular block.

ecg-reel-037.question: A 50-year-old man, routine ECG, normal clinical examination. What is your interpretation?
commentaires: The QRS duration is under 120 ms: the block is not complete.
rSr' in V1 with a QRS of about 100 ms: an incomplete RBBB-type pattern (PTB-XL), a normal variant as the QRS is < 110 ms.
The type 1 pattern involves coved ST elevation ≥ 2 mm followed by a negative T wave in V1–V2, which is absent here.
There is no tall R wave in V1, no right axis deviation and no right ventricular strain.
ecg-reel-037.explication: In V1, the QRS has an rSr' pattern with a small terminal r' wave, and the total QRS duration is about 100 ms; the S wave in V6 and I is slightly widened. According to the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations, incomplete right bundle branch block strictly requires an rsr'/rSR' pattern in V1–V2 with a QRS duration of 110 to 119 ms in adults; with a QRS < 110 ms, as here, this rSr' pattern (annotated "incomplete RBBB" in PTB-XL) is best described as an incomplete RBBB-type pattern: a common variant, of no pathological significance in an asymptomatic individual. The PTB-XL report indeed describes it as a "probable normal variant". The main differential diagnosis not to be missed is the Brugada pattern (ST elevation in V1–V2).
ecg-reel-037.aRetenir: rSr' in V1 with QRS < 120 ms: incomplete RBBB if the QRS is 110–119 ms; below 110 ms, an rSr' pattern that is usually a normal variant.

ecg-reel-038.question: A 75-year-old woman with hypertension, annual ECG. What is the approximate frontal QRS axis?
commentaires: I positive; II, III and aVF negative with an rS pattern: marked left axis deviation, around −60°.
An axis of 0° would give an isodiphasic aVF and a positive lead II.
An axis of +60° would give a strongly positive lead II and a small aVL, the opposite of this tracing.
Right axis deviation would give a negative lead I and a positive lead III.
ecg-reel-038.explication: Quick method: lead I is positive (axis between −90° and +90°) and aVF is negative (axis between 0° and −90°). Lead II is also clearly negative (rS): the axis is therefore beyond −30°. The most isodiphasic lead is aVR (−150°), so the axis is perpendicular to it, i.e. −60° or +120°; as lead I is positive, it is −60°, consistent with III (+120°) being the most negative lead and aVL positive. This marked left axis deviation, with an rS pattern in II, III and aVF, qR in aVL and narrow QRS complexes, meets the criteria for left anterior fascicular block (axis between −45° and −90°, 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS), as annotated in PTB-XL. Calculating the axis is the first step in recognising fascicular block.
ecg-reel-038.aRetenir: Lead I positive + lead II negative = axis beyond −30°; between −45° and −90° with inferior rS complexes, think of left anterior fascicular block.

ecg-reel-039.question: An 81-year-old man, follow-up ECG for hypertension. Which diagnosis accounts for the appearance of the limb leads?
commentaires: Axis beyond −45°, rS in II, III and aVF (S in III > S in II), qR in aVL, narrow QRS complexes.
The inferior leads begin with a small r wave: there is no pathological Q wave.
Left posterior fascicular block produces right axis deviation (≥ +90°), the opposite of this tracing.
The QRS complexes are narrow and V1 does not show the broad QS pattern of LBBB.
ecg-reel-039.explication: The frontal plane shows lead I positive and II, III and aVF negative with an rS pattern, with a deeper S wave in III than in II, and a qR pattern in aVL: the axis is about −50°. The QRS complexes remain narrow. These are the criteria for left anterior fascicular block (2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS). The classic pitfall is confusion with inferior myocardial infarction: in fascicular block, the inferior leads begin with a small r wave (rS); in inferior infarction, they begin with a Q wave (QS or Qr). Isolated LAFB is common in elderly hypertensive patients and does not require specific investigation. PTB-XL annotation: left anterior fascicular block.
ecg-reel-039.aRetenir: LAFB: axis −45° to −90°, inferior rS (small initial r), qR in aVL; an initial Q wave in the inferior leads points to infarction.

ecg-reel-040.question: A 63-year-old woman, routine ECG. Given the frontal axis on this tracing, which diagnoses should be considered?
options: Right ventricular hypertrophy or cor pulmonale
commentaires: Left anterior fascicular block shifts the axis to the left (≤ −45°), the opposite of this tracing.
The axis is deviated to the right (≈ +110°) with rS in I and a dominant R wave in the inferior leads: this is the PTB-XL annotation.
The QRS complexes are narrow and the axis is rightward: no criteria for LBBB.
Left posterior fascicular block is a diagnosis of exclusion: right ventricular strain must be ruled out.
There is neither a short PR interval nor a delta wave.
ecg-reel-040.explication: Lead I is barely negative (rS), while II, III and aVF are clearly positive with R in III > R in II: the frontal axis is about +110°. The QRS complexes are narrow. The 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations define left posterior fascicular block as an axis between +90° and +180°, with an rS pattern in I and aVL and qR in III and aVF, in adults, after exclusion of other causes of right axis deviation: right ventricular hypertrophy or strain (COPD, pulmonary embolism, congenital heart disease), extensive lateral infarction, slender body habitus. It is therefore a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring correlation with clinical and echocardiographic findings. PTB-XL annotation: probable left posterior fascicular block.
ecg-reel-040.aRetenir: Right axis deviation (> +90°): left posterior fascicular block is diagnosed only after excluding a right-sided cause or lateral infarction.

ecg-reel-041.question: An 81-year-old woman with two episodes of brief loss of consciousness without prodrome. What is the most complete interpretation of the conduction disorders?
options: Complete RBBB with a normal axis
Complete RBBB + LAFB + first-degree AV block
Complete LBBB with first-degree AV block
LPFB and Mobitz I second-degree AV block
commentaires: The axis is markedly leftward (II, III and aVF deeply negative): there is associated left anterior fascicular block.
Right-sided delay in V1, axis ≈ −80/−90° with inferior rS complexes, and prolonged PR interval: involvement of all three "fascicles" (in the broad sense).
V1 shows a dominant R wave (right-sided delay), not the QS pattern of LBBB.
The axis is leftward and every P wave is conducted.
ecg-reel-041.explication: In V1–V2, a dominant widened R wave (right-sided delay) and, in I and V6, a broad S wave: complete right bundle branch block (QRS ≈ 130 ms). In the frontal plane, II, III and aVF are deeply negative rS complexes, aVL is positive and I is almost isodiphasic: axis ≈ −80/−90°, i.e. associated left anterior fascicular block (bifascicular block). The PR interval is also prolonged (first-degree AV block, PTB-XL annotation). In a patient with unexplained syncope, bifascicular block raises suspicion of paroxysmal AV block: the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend an EP study (HV measurement) or an implantable loop recorder, and pacing if HV ≥ 70 ms or AV block is documented. First-degree AV block alone does not indicate the level of block.
ecg-reel-041.aRetenir: RBBB + LAFB = bifascicular block; with syncope, paroxysmal AV block must be sought (EP study, implantable loop recorder).

ecg-reel-042.question: An 81-year-old woman being investigated for a fall. How should the intraventricular conduction disorder on this tracing be described?
options: Isolated LAFB, without right bundle block
Bifascicular block: complete RBBB and LAFB
commentaires: The axis is beyond −45°: left anterior fascicular block is also present.
The V1 morphology (terminal R') and the broad S wave in V6 indicate associated RBBB.
Right-sided delay in V1 and frontal axis ≈ −55° with rS in II, III and aVF.
V1 is positive at the end of the QRS: this is right-sided delay.
ecg-reel-042.explication: In V1, an rsR' pattern with a terminal R' and, in I and V6, a widened S wave: complete right bundle branch block. In the frontal plane, I and aVL are positive, while II, III and aVF show an rS pattern with S in III > S in II: axis ≈ −55°, meeting the criterion for left anterior fascicular block. The combination of RBBB + LAFB defines bifascicular block, the most common combination, reflecting extensive conduction system disease. In an asymptomatic patient, it does not justify pacing; in the case of unexplained syncope, investigation for paroxysmal AV block is recommended (ESC 2021). PTB-XL annotation: RBBB + LAFB.
ecg-reel-042.aRetenir: The most common bifascicular block: RBBB + LAFB; no pacing without symptoms or documented AV block.

ecg-reel-043.question: An 85-year-old man, asymptomatic, ECG before cataract surgery. What is the appropriate management of the conduction disorder on this tracing?
options: No pacing; clinical and ECG follow-up
commentaires: Asymptomatic bifascicular block is not an indication for pacing.
The risk of perioperative complete AV block is low and does not justify routine prophylactic pacing.
An EP study is reserved for bifascicular block with unexplained syncope.
Asymptomatic bifascicular block without AV block: pacing is not indicated (ESC 2021, class III).
ecg-reel-043.explication: The tracing shows complete right bundle branch block (rsR' in V1, broad S wave in I and V6) associated with left anterior fascicular block (marked left axis deviation with rS in II, III and aVF): this is bifascicular block, in sinus rhythm, without AV block. In an asymptomatic patient, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend neither pacing (class III) nor a routine EP study; the latter is reserved for patients with unexplained syncope. The patient should be told which symptoms should prompt medical attention (presyncope, syncope). PTB-XL annotation: RBBB + LAFB, bifascicular block.
ecg-reel-043.aRetenir: Asymptomatic bifascicular block: neither pacing nor a routine EP study; patient information and follow-up.

ecg-reel-044.question: A 78-year-old man, follow-up ECG. True or false: this tracing shows complete right bundle branch block with a normal frontal axis.
commentaires: Right-sided delay is indeed present, but the axis is markedly leftward (rS in II, III and aVF): there is associated left anterior fascicular block.
The frontal axis shows marked left deviation (≈ −75°): RBBB + LAFB, i.e. bifascicular block.
ecg-reel-044.explication: In V1, the broad terminal R' wave indicates complete right bundle branch block; in I and V5–V6, the terminal S wave is widened. But the axis is not normal: I and aVL are positive, while II, III and aVF show an rS pattern, placing the axis at around −70/−80°, meeting the criterion for left anterior fascicular block. The full diagnosis is therefore bifascicular block (RBBB + LAFB), annotated as such in PTB-XL. Failing to calculate the axis in the presence of RBBB means missing this combination, which carries a different prognostic significance in the event of syncope.
ecg-reel-044.aRetenir: RBBB can only be called "isolated" after checking the frontal axis.

ecg-reel-045.question: A 69-year-old woman with progressive exertional dyspnoea. What is the conduction disorder?
commentaires: There is no terminal R' wave in V1 and no broad S wave in I and V6.
Isolated LVH does not produce a QRS ≥ 120 ms with notched R waves and no septal q wave.
QRS ≥ 120 ms, broad QS in V1–V3, broad notched R wave in I, aVL and V6 with no septal q wave.
The PR interval is not short and there is no delta wave.
ecg-reel-045.explication: The QRS complexes are wide (≈ 130–140 ms), with a deep QS pattern in V1–V3 and, in I, aVL and V6, a broad, notched ("plateau") R wave with no septal q wave. Repolarisation is discordant (ST-T opposite to the QRS), secondary to the block. These are the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS criteria for complete LBBB. LBBB is almost always a marker of structural heart disease (hypertensive, ischaemic, dilated): in a breathless patient, echocardiography is essential, and LBBB with reduced LVEF may warrant cardiac resynchronisation therapy. PTB-XL annotation: complete LBBB.
ecg-reel-045.aRetenir: Complete LBBB: QRS ≥ 120 ms, QS/rS in V1, broad notched R wave in I, aVL and V6 with no septal q wave, discordant repolarisation.

ecg-reel-046.question: An 81-year-old woman being investigated for heart failure. Which statements about this tracing are correct?
options: There is complete left bundle branch block
The ST elevation in V1–V3 establishes acute infarction
The frontal axis is deviated to the left
A delta wave explains the QRS widening
This is right bundle branch block
commentaires: QRS ≈ 140 ms, deep QS in V1–V3 and broad R waves in I and aVL.
Moderate discordant ST elevation in V1–V3 is expected in LBBB and is not sufficient to diagnose infarction.
Lead I positive and II, III and aVF negative: axis beyond −30°.
There is neither a short PR interval nor initial QRS slurring.
V1 is negative (QS): this is left-sided delay.
ecg-reel-046.explication: The QRS is wide (≈ 140 ms), with a QS pattern in V1–V3 and broad R waves in I and aVL: complete left bundle branch block. The axis is deviated to the left (I positive; II, III and aVF negative), a common association reflecting more extensive disease of the left conduction system. The ST elevation in V1–V3 and the T waves opposite to the QRS are secondary changes; in the case of chest pain, the diagnosis of infarction in LBBB relies on specific criteria (Sgarbossa criteria: concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm, concordant ST depression in V1–V3, excessively discordant ST elevation). LBBB + heart failure with LVEF ≤ 35%: consider cardiac resynchronisation therapy (ESC 2021). PTB-XL annotation: LBBB.
ecg-reel-046.aRetenir: In LBBB, discordant repolarisation is expected: ischaemia must be sought using specific criteria (Sgarbossa).

ecg-reel-047.question: An 81-year-old woman with dyspnoea and irregular palpitations. What is your interpretation?
options: Atrial fibrillation with left bundle branch block
commentaires: Irregularly irregular RR intervals with no P waves, wide QRS complexes of constant LBBB-type morphology.
The rate is ≈ 74 bpm and the QRS complexes have a constant morphology: this is neither a tachycardia nor a polymorphic pattern.
There are no sinus P waves and all the QRS complexes have the same morphology.
The RR intervals are completely irregular, which is not consistent with a ventricular rhythm.
ecg-reel-047.explication: The RR intervals are irregularly irregular (0.66 to 1.13 s), with no identifiable P waves: atrial fibrillation at ≈ 74 bpm. All the QRS complexes have the same wide morphology (≈ 140 ms), with QS in V1–V3, a broad notched R wave in I, aVL and V6 and left axis deviation: left bundle branch block. An irregular wide-QRS rhythm with constant morphology is AF conducted with bundle branch block until proven otherwise; VT is usually regular, and pre-excited AF produces QRS complexes of varying width and very short cycles. PTB-XL annotation: AF + LBBB.
ecg-reel-047.aRetenir: Irregular rhythm with identical wide QRS complexes: think of AF with bundle branch block; varying QRS width and very short cycles: think of pre-excited AF.

ecg-reel-048.question: A 73-year-old woman, admission ECG for decompensated heart failure. What is the underlying rhythm and why are the QRS complexes wide?
ecg-reel-048.reponseAttendue: Atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular RR intervals, no P waves) conducted with complete left bundle branch block (wide QRS, QS in V1–V3, broad R wave in I and aVL, left axis deviation).
ecg-reel-048.explication: The rhythm is irregularly irregular (RR 0.68 to 1.21 s, ≈ 71 bpm) with no organised P waves: atrial fibrillation. All the QRS complexes have the same wide morphology (≈ 130–140 ms): deep QS in V1–V3, broad R wave in I and aVL, marked left axis deviation (II, III and aVF negative), discordant repolarisation. The widening is due to complete left bundle branch block, not to a ventricular origin. The combination of AF + LBBB in a patient with heart failure calls for assessment of LVEF; if LVEF is reduced, a rhythm control strategy and, depending on the case, cardiac resynchronisation therapy may be considered. PTB-XL annotation: AF + LBBB.
ecg-reel-048.aRetenir: Wide QRS complexes of constant morphology in an irregular rhythm: identify the rhythm (AF) and the conduction (bundle branch block) separately.

ecg-reel-049.question: A 63-year-old man, pre-operative ECG, with a history of palpitations in his youth. What is your interpretation?
options: Incomplete left bundle branch block and ventricular hypertrophy
Old inferior myocardial infarction with Q waves
Left anterior fascicular block with first-degree AV block
commentaires: The widening starts at the very beginning of the QRS, immediately after the P wave, with no isoelectric PR segment: this is a delta wave.
The negative waves in III and aVF are negative delta waves (pseudo-Q waves), not infarct Q waves.
The PR interval is not prolonged (≈ 130 ms) and runs straight into a delta wave.
P wave running straight into initial QRS slurring (delta wave), clearly visible in I, aVL and V2–V4.
ecg-reel-049.explication: The PR interval is at the lower limit of normal (≈ 130 ms, "rather short" according to the PTB-XL report) rather than strictly short (< 120 ms), but the P wave runs straight into the QRS with no isoelectric PR segment, and the QRS upstroke is slurred from the outset (delta wave), clearly in I, aVL and V2–V4, where the R wave is tall from V1 and dominant in V2. In III and aVF, the delta wave is negative and mimics a Q wave (inferior pseudo-infarction). Repolarisation is secondarily altered. A dominant R wave in V1 suggests a left-sided accessory pathway; with a distant left lateral pathway, the PR interval is often not frankly short, so the delta wave is the key sign. In a symptomatic patient (palpitations), the 2019 ESC guidelines recommend an EP study and, in most cases, ablation of the pathway. PTB-XL annotation: WPW.
ecg-reel-049.aRetenir: Pre-excitation = short PR (sometimes only at the lower limit of normal) + delta wave + QRS widened by fusion; negative delta waves can mimic infarct Q waves.

ecg-reel-050.question: A 27-year-old woman being investigated for palpitations. True or false: the initial negative waves in III and aVF on this tracing indicate an old inferior myocardial infarction.
commentaires: These are negative delta waves (pseudo-Q waves) due to pre-excitation, not infarct Q waves.
The short PR interval and the initial QRS slurring, positive in I and aVL, identify pre-excitation: the inferior "Q waves" are negative delta waves.
ecg-reel-050.explication: In I and aVL, the very tall R wave begins with slurring (delta wave) immediately following the P wave: short PR interval and pre-excitation. In III and aVF, the same delta wave is negative, producing a broad QS pattern that can be mistaken for inferior infarction: this is the classic WPW "pseudo-infarction" pattern. In a 27-year-old woman with no risk factors, pre-excitation must be recognised and infarction must not be wrongly diagnosed. In a symptomatic patient, an EP study and ablation of the accessory pathway are recommended (ESC 2019). PTB-XL annotation: WPW (short PR, delta waves).
ecg-reel-050.aRetenir: With "Q waves" in a young person, look for a short PR interval and a delta wave: WPW pseudo-infarction.

ecg-reel-051.question: A 20-year-old man with episodes of rapid palpitations. Which statements about this tracing and its management are correct?
options: The wide QRS complexes reflect right bundle branch block
The PR interval is short, with a delta wave
In pre-excited AF, IV AV nodal blocking drugs are contraindicated
An EP study and ablation of the accessory pathway are recommended
commentaires: The widening is initial (delta wave), not terminal as in right bundle branch block.
The QRS upstroke is slurred from the end of the P wave, very clearly in II, III and aVF.
Each QRS is preceded by a sinus P wave.
Verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin (and adenosine) can promote rapid conduction over the pathway and VF.
In a symptomatic patient, catheter ablation is the recommended treatment (ESC 2019, class I).
ecg-reel-051.explication: Sinus rhythm at ≈ 50 bpm; the PR interval is short and the QRS begins with a very large delta wave, positive in II, III, aVF and V1–V3, negative in I and aVL (apparent right axis). The QRS is widened by fusion between activation via the accessory pathway and via the normal conduction system. In this symptomatic patient, the 2019 ESC guidelines recommend an EP study and ablation (class I). The major risk is pre-excited AF conducted very rapidly over the pathway, which can degenerate into VF: AV nodal blocking drugs are then contraindicated, and electrical cardioversion is recommended if the patient is unstable, while IV ibutilide or procainamide should be considered if stable (class IIa). PTB-XL annotation: WPW.
ecg-reel-051.aRetenir: Symptomatic WPW: ablation; pre-excited AF: never give an AV nodal blocking drug; cardiovert if unstable.

ecg-reel-052.question: A 34-year-old man, pre-employment ECG. What abnormality is seen at the start of the QRS complexes in V2–V3, and what is the diagnosis?
ecg-reel-052.reponseAttendue: Initial slurring of the QRS upstroke (delta wave) immediately after the P wave, with a short PR interval: ventricular pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern).
ecg-reel-052.explication: In V2–V3, the QRS begins immediately after the P wave with a slow, slurred upstroke (delta wave) before the rapid deflection: the PR interval is short and the QRS widened. The tall R waves from V2 onwards and the R wave in V1 suggest a left-sided accessory pathway (so-called "type A" pattern). The repolarisation abnormalities (negative T waves in V2–V3) are secondary to pre-excitation. In an asymptomatic individual, the 2019 ESC guidelines propose risk stratification (EP study, class IIa; exercise testing looking for abrupt loss of pre-excitation), especially in high-risk occupations. PTB-XL annotation: WPW.
ecg-reel-052.aRetenir: Delta wave = initial slurring of the QRS immediately after the P wave; in asymptomatic individuals, stratify the risk of the accessory pathway.

ecg-reel-053.question: A 76-year-old man with a pacemaker of unknown type. What is the most likely ventricular pacing site?
options: Left ventricle via the coronary sinus
commentaires: Epicardial LV pacing gives a right-sided delay pattern (dominant R wave in V1), often with right axis deviation.
Spike followed by a wide QRS with a left-sided delay pattern (QS in V1–V3) and a superior axis (II, III and aVF negative).
Selective His bundle pacing produces a narrow QRS identical to the intrinsic QRS.
Atrial pacing alone would be followed by a P wave and then a narrow intrinsic QRS.
ecg-reel-053.explication: Each QRS is preceded by a ventricular spike at a fixed rate (≈ 70 bpm). The paced QRS is wide, with a left-sided delay pattern (QS in V1–V3, R in I and aVL) and a superior frontal axis (II, III and aVF negative): activation starts in the RV apical region and travels up towards the base, which is typical of RV apical or low septal pacing. Epicardial LV pacing would give a dominant R wave in V1; conduction system pacing (His, left bundle branch) a narrow QRS or an incomplete right bundle branch delay pattern. PTB-XL annotation: normal paced rhythm.
ecg-reel-053.aRetenir: RV apical pacing: wide LBBB-like QRS with a superior axis; LV pacing: dominant R wave in V1.

ecg-reel-054.question: A 75-year-old woman with a pacemaker, routine follow-up ECG, no chest pain. True or false: the left-sided delay pattern with T waves opposite to the QRS seen on this tracing is expected with right ventricular pacing and does not, by itself, indicate ischaemia.
commentaires: RV pacing produces slow LBBB-type activation with secondarily discordant repolarisation.
ST-T discordance is the rule with RV pacing: it does not in itself indicate ischaemia.
ecg-reel-054.explication: Each QRS is preceded by a spike, at ≈ 80 bpm. The QRS complexes are wide with a left-sided delay pattern (QS in V1–V3) and a superior axis: right ventricular pacing. As in left bundle branch block, abnormal depolarisation leads to "secondary" repolarisation that is discordant with the QRS (ST elevation in V1–V3, negative T waves in I and aVL). These abnormalities should not be interpreted as ischaemia; in the case of chest pain, specific criteria (modified Sgarbossa) are required, with limited sensitivity. Another pitfall: negative T waves persisting after return to intrinsic rhythm ("cardiac memory") are not necessarily ischaemic. PTB-XL annotation: normal paced rhythm.
ecg-reel-054.aRetenir: RV pacing: discordant repolarisation is expected; ischaemia can only be assessed with specific criteria.

ecg-reel-055.question: A 77-year-old man with a pacemaker, follow-up ECG some time after implantation. Which pacemaker function is shown on this tracing?
options: Ventricular pacing alone in VVI mode
Atrial pacing alone with intrinsic conduction
commentaires: An atrial spike precedes each ventricular spike: the atrium is also paced.
Two spikes per cycle: an atrial spike then, ≈ 190 ms later, a ventricular spike followed by a wide QRS.
The QRS complexes are wide and preceded by a ventricular spike: they are paced.
Each ventricular spike is followed by a wide captured QRS.
ecg-reel-055.explication: On the lead II strip and in V1, two spikes can be seen in each cycle: a first (atrial) spike, followed about 190 ms later by a second (ventricular) spike immediately followed by a wide LBBB-type QRS with left axis deviation. The rate is ≈ 62 bpm. This is sequential dual-chamber pacing (atrial paced – ventricular paced), the interval between the two spikes corresponding to the programmed AV delay. The paced P wave is of low amplitude. This mode preserves AV synchrony; when AV conduction is intact, algorithms to minimise ventricular pacing are recommended. PTB-XL annotation: "normal dual-chamber pacing, rate 62".
ecg-reel-055.aRetenir: Two spikes per cycle (A then V) separated by the AV delay: sequential dual-chamber pacing.

ecg-reel-056.question: A 79-year-old woman with a pacemaker implanted for complete AV block. Which pacemaker behaviour does this tracing illustrate?
options: Atrial pacing alone with intrinsic AV conduction
Loss of ventricular capture with an escape rhythm
commentaires: The rate varies with the atrial rhythm and the spikes consistently follow a P wave.
The QRS complexes are wide and preceded by a ventricular spike: they are paced.
Each ventricular spike is followed by a wide captured QRS.
Each ventricular spike follows a P wave at a fixed interval, and the rate (≈ 94 bpm) tracks the atrial rhythm.
ecg-reel-056.explication: Each wide QRS, with a left-sided delay pattern and a superior axis (RV pacing), is preceded by a ventricular spike, which is itself preceded by a P wave at a constant interval (≈ 150 ms). No atrial spike is visible before these P waves. The ventricular rate (≈ 94 bpm) therefore tracks atrial activity: the pacemaker senses the atrium and paces the ventricle after the AV delay (VDD/DDD operation, "P-synchronous"). In a patient with complete AV block, this is the expected behaviour, maintaining AV synchrony and sinus-driven rate adaptation. PTB-XL annotation: regular paced rhythm, normal function.
ecg-reel-056.aRetenir: Sensed P wave followed by a V spike at a fixed delay: P-synchronous ventricular pacing (VDD/DDD), which tracks the sinus rate.

ecg-reel-057.question: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing, poorly controlled hypertension. Calculate the Sokolow-Lyon index on this tracing and draw your conclusion.
ecg-reel-057.reponseAttendue: SV1 (≈ 1.9 mV) + RV5 (≈ 4.8 mV) ≈ 6.5–7 mV, well above 3.5 mV: left ventricular hypertrophy, here with strain-type repolarisation abnormalities (ST depression and asymmetric negative T waves in V4–V6).
ecg-reel-057.explication: The Sokolow-Lyon index adds the S wave in V1 to the tallest R wave in V5 or V6; it is positive above 3.5 mV (35 mm). Here, SV1 ≈ 19 mm and RV5 ≈ 48 mm (the R wave runs beyond the lead's display area): index ≈ 67 mm. The Cornell criteria are also positive in this woman (RaVL + SV3 > 2.0 mV). Downsloping ST depression with an asymmetric negative T wave in V4–V6 and I corresponds to the classic "strain" pattern, associated with more severe LVH and a less favourable prognosis. Voltage criteria have good specificity but low sensitivity: echocardiography remains the reference investigation. PTB-XL annotation: LVH with repolarisation abnormalities.
ecg-reel-057.aRetenir: Sokolow-Lyon = SV1 + RV5 or RV6 > 3.5 mV; a strain pattern (ST-T) indicates more severe LVH.

ecg-reel-058.question: A 75-year-old woman with known aortic stenosis and exertional dyspnoea. What is the most likely interpretation of the lateral ST-T abnormalities?
commentaires: Markedly increased voltages with downsloping ST and asymmetric negative T waves in V4–V6: strain pattern.
These abnormalities accompany LVH voltages and have the typical strain appearance; ACS requires a compatible clinical and biochemical context.
Pericarditis produces diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, which is absent here.
Digoxin effect produces "scooped" ST segments with a short QT, without LVH voltages.
ecg-reel-058.explication: Voltages are markedly increased: R in V5 ≈ 3.9 mV, S in V1 ≈ 1.3 mV (Sokolow-Lyon ≈ 5.2 mV), tall R waves in II and aVF. In V4–V6, the ST segment is depressed and downsloping, followed by an asymmetric negative T wave: the LVH "strain" pattern. In the context of aortic stenosis, this is the electrical expression of marked pressure-overload LVH; the strain pattern is associated with myocardial fibrosis and a worse prognosis. Interpreting superimposed ischaemia on such a tracing is difficult and relies on the clinical picture, troponin and comparison with previous ECGs. PTB-XL annotation: LVH, ST-T abnormalities.
ecg-reel-058.aRetenir: High voltages + downsloping ST and asymmetric negative T waves laterally: LVH with strain, not ACS by default.

ecg-reel-059.question: A 73-year-old woman with hypertension. Which ECG criterion for left ventricular hypertrophy is met on this tracing?
options: R in I + S in III > 2.5 mV
commentaires: RaVL ≈ 0.4 mV + SV3 ≈ 1.45 mV ≈ 1.9 mV: just below the female threshold of 2.0 mV.
The R wave in aVL measures about 0.4 mV.
R in I ≈ 1.0 mV and S in III almost zero: the sum is far from 2.5 mV.
ecg-reel-059.explication: The tall R waves are in the precordial leads: RV5 ≈ 37–38 mm and SV1 ≈ 12 mm (SV2 ≈ 20 mm), giving a Sokolow-Lyon index ≈ 50 mm, which is positive (> 35 mm). In contrast, the limb lead voltages are modest: RaVL ≈ 4 mm, R I + S III ≈ 10 mm, and the Cornell voltage (RaVL + SV3) ≈ 19 mm remains just below the female threshold (20 mm). This example shows that the various criteria are not concordant and that their sensitivity is low; echocardiography confirms or refutes LVH. Voltage criteria can also be falsely positive in slim individuals. PTB-XL annotation: precordial voltage criteria for LVH.
ecg-reel-059.aRetenir: ECG voltage criteria for LVH are specific but insensitive and often discordant: echocardiography settles the question.

ecg-reel-060.question: A 73-year-old woman with a history of prolonged chest pain several years ago that was never investigated. Which diagnosis best accounts for the appearance of leads II, III and aVF?
options: Pre-excitation with a negative delta wave
commentaires: Fascicular block gives an rS pattern with a small initial r wave, not a QS.
The QRS complexes are narrow and V1 does not show a broad QS.
The PR interval is not short and there is no initial QRS slurring.
QS complexes (no initial r wave) in II, III and aVF: inferior infarct Q waves.
ecg-reel-060.explication: In II, III and aVF, the QRS complexes are of QS type: they begin straight away with a negative deflection, without a small initial r wave, and the axis is markedly leftward. The absence of an initial r wave points to inferior infarct Q waves rather than left anterior fascicular block (which gives an rS pattern). The inferior ST segment remains slightly elevated with a low-amplitude T wave, a common appearance in old infarction. According to the Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction, Q waves ≥ 30 ms in two contiguous leads (or QS complexes) are consistent with prior infarction, to be confirmed by imaging. PTB-XL annotation: inferior myocardial infarction.
ecg-reel-060.aRetenir: Left axis deviation with inferior QS complexes (no initial r): inferior infarction; inferior rS complexes: left anterior fascicular block.

ecg-reel-061.question: A 73-year-old man, follow-up ECG, with a poorly documented history of coronary disease. True or false: the QS pattern from V1 to V3 on this tracing, with normal QRS duration, is typical of complete left bundle branch block.
commentaires: LBBB requires a QRS ≥ 120 ms with broad notched R waves in I, aVL and V6, which are absent here.
QS in V1–V3 with non-widened QRS complexes: old anteroseptal infarction (PTB-XL annotation).
ecg-reel-061.explication: In V1, V2 and V3, the complexes are of QS type, with no R-wave progression, followed by persistent ST elevation with positive T waves. The QRS complexes are not widened (< 120 ms) and there is no broad notched R wave in I, aVL or V6: this is not LBBB. This appearance corresponds to an old anteroseptal infarction; persistent ST elevation over the infarcted area may suggest a ventricular aneurysm, to be looked for on echocardiography. Always compare with previous tracings so as not to mistake this residual ST elevation for acute infarction. PTB-XL annotation: anteroseptal infarction.
ecg-reel-061.aRetenir: QS in V1–V3 with narrow QRS complexes: anteroseptal infarction; LBBB requires a QRS ≥ 120 ms with a broad notched R wave in the lateral leads.
